alamut_1256.stores.dip_done: Wine, vinegar, honey and water, and every tank near the brim. No milk. And no castle starved out: Alamut still had stores for years when it was given up. When the soldiers came to the tanks, one of them fell into the honey and was nearly drowned.
alamut_1256.stores.tunnel_shut: A wide, high tunnel climbs through the rock towards the library. A tally board hangs across it: the stores are to be counted before anything else is moved.
alamut_1256.stores.jars: Great jars along the wall, sealed: grain, lentils, dried fruit, laid in for a long siege that never came.
alamut_1256.stores.lamps: Lamps in niches along the gallery, still burning. The garrison left in good order.
alamut_1256.library.leaves: Folded sheets on the floor that should not be here yet: pages of Juvayni's History of the World Conqueror, written some four years from now, loose from their sewing. In a manuscript the first word of each page is written again at the foot of the page before, the catchword, so a binder can gather the sheets in order.
alamut_1256.library.leaves_done: The sheets gathered in order, every catchword meeting its page.
alamut_1256.library.quire_done: The sheets read through. [[juvayni]], the Mongol prince's secretary, came up to see [[library]] whose fame had spread through every land. He kept the Qur'ans, the choice books and the instruments. The rest he gave to the fire, and Hasan's own story with them, once he had read it and taken what he needed.
alamut_1256.library.niches: Tall niches from floor to ceiling, most of them already emptied. A few books still lie on their sides.
alamut_1256.library.tusi: A writing box and a worn cushion: a scholar's corner. [[tusi]], the astronomer, lived among the Nizaris for some twenty years and wrote here. When [[hulagu]] came, he counselled the imam to give up, and went over to the Mongols; three years later he began the great observatory at Maragha, with books from the conquered libraries.
alamut_1256.library.later: A paper that should not be here yet, from long after. The name hashishi, it says, was an insult other Muslims used for the Nizaris, meaning rabble; no record says they took [[hashish]]. A French scholar tied "assassin" to the drug in 1809. The Nizaris did kill their enemies: the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, in 1092, is the best known. But the garden and the drug were travellers' tales. Gerdkuh held out until 1270, and in 1275 a Nizari band took Alamut back for a year.
alamut_1256.library.kursi: The throne of an astrolabe on its stand, empty. The instruments were taken out and kept.
alamut_1256.library.keeper_note: Tucked under the empty throne, a slip in the keeper's hand: "A traveller who never climbed here wrote a garden, and the world believed him for seven hundred years. The man who burned the books is the one who told us what they were. Keep his pages too: they are all that is left."
alamut_1256.library.kursi_done: The empty throne, where the keeper's slip lay.
alamut_1256.quire.l1: When the castle was given up, I asked leave of the king to go up and see the library, whose fame had spread through every land.
alamut_1256.quire.l2: Its books had been gathered over many years: shelves of manuscripts on every science, and instruments for measuring the sky.
alamut_1256.quire.l3: From among them I took out copies of the Qur'an and other choice books, as many as could be carried down.
alamut_1256.quire.l4: Likewise I picked out the instruments: the thrones of astrolabes, armillary spheres, astrolabes whole and in parts.
alamut_1256.quire.l5: Among the books was the life of Hasan-i Sabbah, their first master. I read it through and took from it what I needed for this history.
alamut_1256.quire.l6: The rest, which I judged to belong to their heresy and error, I gave to the fire, and his life with them.
alamut_1256.quire.l7: Then the walls were pulled down. They were plastered and roofed with lead, and would not fall to the pick; fires were lit to bring them down.
alamut_1256.quire.l8: Here ends the account of the taking of Alamut, from the History of the World Conqueror of Ata-Malik Juvayni.
alamut_1256.label.s1: The fortress kept {1}, not a garden; {2} gave its books to the fire in {3}.
alamut_1256.label.done: The colophon is written and the book is finished, its last line narrowing to a point, as a scribe's would.
alamut_1256.ending.given: Alamut was given up in December 1256. Its walls were pulled down, and its library burned.
alamut_1256.ending.record: Hasan's own story is lost. What we know of it comes from the pages of the man who burned it.
hint.alamut_1256.start.1: Read the order pinned to the gate.
hint.alamut_1256.start.2: It tells how the castle came to be given up.
hint.alamut_1256.tower.1: Climb the tower on the right of the court.
hint.alamut_1256.tower.2: Look for what the commander left behind when he went down.
hint.alamut_1256.stores.1: The keys open the storerooms, on the left of the court.
hint.alamut_1256.stores.2: Dip each tank in the storerooms.
hint.alamut_1256.library.1: The tunnel in the storerooms climbs to the library.
hint.alamut_1256.library.2: Gather the loose sheets on the library floor.
hint.alamut_1256.later.1: Something new lies in the scholar's corner of the library.
hint.alamut_1256.later.2: Read it: what was the legend, and what is the record?
hint.alamut_1256.write_seal.1: The colophon waits at the gate.
hint.alamut_1256.write_seal.2: Tap the order on the gate.
hint.alamut_1256.dip.1: Lower the reed slowly until it meets the surface, then draw it out and watch how it drips.
hint.alamut_1256.dip.2: Honey falls in a slow thread, vinegar in quick pale drops; wine drips dark, water clear. Milk would be white.
hint.alamut_1256.dip.3: Wine, vinegar, honey, water, from left to right; and the stores were full.
hint.alamut_1256.quire.1: Each page's first word is written again at the foot of the page before.
hint.alamut_1256.quire.2: The outermost sheet holds the first page and the last. Turn a sheet over to swap its two leaves.
hint.alamut_1256.quire.3: From the outside in, the sheets hold pages 1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5.
hint.alamut_1256.jar_label.1: What did the fortress really keep?
hint.alamut_1256.jar_label.2: Who chose which books would burn, and when?
episode.great_zimbabwe_1871.title: Great Zimbabwe, 1871
episode.great_zimbabwe_1871.teaser: A city of stone without mortar, a splinter of scented wood, and a visitor who gave it all to a queen from a book.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.wall: The outer wall of the great enclosure, taller than five people, curving away out of sight. Granite blocks in level courses and no mortar at all; along the top, a band of slabs set slanting in a zigzag, the chevrons.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.breach: Here the wall has slumped: a gap above the lowest course, and its fallen blocks heaped in the entrance below. The same split granite, in two lengths. Laid back course by course, it would stand again, and clear the way in.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.breach_done: The gap is closed, course over course, every joint covered by the block above it.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.courses_done: The wall stands, dry, every joint crossed by the block above, the chevrons leaning in turn along the top. Whoever built this knew the stone: the granite of these hills splits in sheets, and the builders broke it into blocks a person can carry. The entrance below is clear.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.entrance_shut: The narrow entrance in the wall, choked with fallen blocks.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.fig: A wild fig has rooted in the top of the wall, its roots running down over the stones.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.keeper_note: Under the fig's roots, a slip in the keeper's hand: "He smelled his pencil and gave the city to a queen from a book. The stones never said a word; they did not need to. Stand them up again, one over two, and they say who laid them."
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.fig_done: The fig's roots over the stones, where the keeper's slip lay.
great_zimbabwe_1871.valley.seal_needed: On the wall, below the chevrons, a map's cartouche waits to be written: who built this, from when, and what the lintel was.
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.notebook: The notebook of [[mauch]], open at September 1871. The hunter Adam Render brought him here; Render was sure the people of the land could not have built such walls, and Mauch agrees. This is [[ophir]], he writes, where [[solomon]] had his gold, in [[bc10]]; [[phoenicians]] laid these stones, and the round building was the palace of [[sheba]].
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.pencil: His pencil, worn short, its wood reddish and scented. He held the splinter beside it and found a "great similarity": [[cedar]], he decided, which only the Phoenicians could have brought.
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.splinter_wait: A splinter of reddish wood in a twist of paper, labelled in Mauch's hand: "from the fallen lintel". Reddish, scented, untouched by insects, he notes.
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.splinter: The splinter, and Mauch's hand lens. Beside them, a key to woods: pairs of statements, and the true one leads on. Mauch never put the splinter under the lens.
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.identify_done: Not cedar. Under the lens the splinter is full of fine pores, as no conifer's wood ever is: [[tambootie]], Spirostachys africana, a scented hardwood that grows on this plateau and that insects leave alone. No one had to bring it from anywhere.
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.rifle: A hunter's rifle against the tent pole. Adam Render, who has lived in this country for years, came on the ruins in 1867 and led Mauch to them.
great_zimbabwe_1871.camp.msasa: Msasa trees on the slope, red with new leaves: September, the end of the dry season.
great_zimbabwe_1871.enclosure.tower: The conical tower: solid stone, round, nine metres high, with no door and no room inside. No one knows what it meant.
great_zimbabwe_1871.enclosure.passage: A narrow passage between two high walls, wide enough for one person, running towards the tower.
great_zimbabwe_1871.enclosure.lintel: A doorway in the inner wall has fallen in. Among its stones lies the lintel, a beam of dark wood, with a fresh cut where someone has taken a splinter from it.
great_zimbabwe_1871.enclosure.report: Papers that should not be here yet, decades of them. 1902: the curator Richard Hall digs out some twelve feet of deposits to rid the site, he writes, of the "filth and decadence" of the people who lived in it, and throws away the evidence. 1905: David Randall-MacIver finds only African work, and goods brought from afar in the Middle Ages: Persian beads, Chinese porcelain, a copper coin of Kilwa. 1929: Gertrude Caton-Thompson: "every detail in plan, building, and contents seems African Bantu." Built by [[shona]], from [[c11]] to the 15th.
great_zimbabwe_1871.hill.birds: On a terrace among the boulders, carved birds of soapstone stand on tall stone pillars: birds of prey with folded wings. In 1871 all eight are still here.
great_zimbabwe_1871.hill.view: Below, the great enclosure: an oval of stone in the valley, the tower's top showing over the wall. Cicadas in the dry grass.
great_zimbabwe_1871.hill.boulders: Great boulders of granite, their skins splitting off in sheets: the stone the walls are made of.
great_zimbabwe_1871.hill.later: A paper that should not be here yet. In 1889 a hunter cut one of these birds from its pillar and sold it to [[rhodes]]; in 1891 Theodore Bent took four more. In 1970 the Rhodesian government forbade its own publications to say plainly that Africans had built the city, and the archaeologist Peter Garlake left the country in protest. In 1980 the country took the city's name: Zimbabwe, "houses of stone". South Africa sent four birds back in 1981, Berlin a piece of one in 2003; the last came home in April 2026.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.pores_yes: In the cross-section: pores, open vessels, among the fibres.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.pores_no: In the cross-section: no pores, only even rows of small cells.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.conifer_scent: Reddish heartwood, with a strong scent.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.conifer_plain: Pale yellowish wood, with little scent.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.size_fine: The pores are fine, seen only under the lens.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.size_large: The pores are large, seen without a lens, in rings.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.scent_yes: Dark heartwood, scented and oily; insects leave it alone.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.scent_no: Plain wood without scent, soon eaten by borers.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.cedar_note: A conifer: its wood is reddish and scented, as Mauch said, but like every conifer's it has no pores. This splinter has.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.softwood_note: A conifer with pale, plain wood: no pores, little scent. Nothing like this splinter.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.ringwood_note: Its pores are large, plain to the eye, in rings. This splinter's pores show only under the lens.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.plainwood_note: Without scent, soon riddled by borers. This splinter is scented, and insects had not touched it.
great_zimbabwe_1871.key.tambootie_note: Spirostachys africana: a hardwood of this plateau, fine-pored, its heartwood dark, scented and oily, left alone by insects.
great_zimbabwe_1871.label.s1: Built by {1} from {2}; the lintel Mauch called cedar was {3}.
great_zimbabwe_1871.label.done: The cartouche is written, where the old maps wrote Ophir.
great_zimbabwe_1871.ending.built: Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona, from the 11th century to the 15th, and was the seat of a kingdom that traded gold to the coast.
great_zimbabwe_1871.ending.name: In 1980 a country took its name. In April 2026 the last of its stone birds came home.

hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.lintel.2: Find the fallen doorway and its lintel.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.wood.1: Mauch's splinter is in the camp.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.wood.2: Look at it under the lens, and follow the key.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.report.1: Papers wait in the enclosure, by the tower.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.birds.1: Climb the hill, to the birds.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.birds.2: A paper lies among the boulders.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.write_seal.1: The cartouche waits on the wall, below the chevrons.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.write_seal.2: Tap the top of the wall in the valley.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.courses.1: Lay each course from the left. No block may end where a block ends in the course below.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.courses.2: Two of the courses must begin with a short block; they need all four short ones between them.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.courses.3: From the bottom: short, long, long, short; then three long; then short, long, long, short. Then tap the slabs until they lean in turn.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.identify.1: Look at the splinter under the lens before anything else.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.identify.2: It has pores, fine ones. No conifer has pores, so it is not cedar.
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.jar_label.1: Who built the city of stone?
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.jar_label.2: From which century? And what wood was the lintel?
hint.great_zimbabwe_1871.jar_label.3: The ancestors of the Shona; the 11th century; tambootie.
episode.dyatlov_1959.title: Dyatlov Pass, 1959
episode.dyatlov_1959.teaser: A tent cut open from inside, footprints going down in a line, and sixty years of monsters for a night no one saw.
dyatlov_1959.slope.tent: The tent, half under snow on its platform below the shoulder, pitched across the slope. Its side is slit open in long cuts, from the inside. Skis laid under the floor, boots inside, coats inside. They left in the night with almost nothing.
dyatlov_1959.slope.tracks: Footprints going down the slope: eight or nine people, in socks, in one felt boot, barefoot. They stand as small columns of pressed snow above the wind-scoured surface. A walking pace, in a line, close together, for about five hundred metres, towards [[cedar]] at the edge of the forest.
dyatlov_1959.slope.shoulder: Above the tent, a small shoulder in the slope, and under it snow the wind has packed hard, drifted down from the ridge.
dyatlov_1959.slope.pit_wait: Beside the tent the snow is deep and layered. There is nothing here to dig it with, or test it.
dyatlov_1959.slope.pit: A snow kit that should not be here yet: a shovel, a saw, a pencil and a knife. Beside the tent, a pit dug down through the snow, its wall cut smooth.
dyatlov_1959.slope.pit_done: The pit, and the column that broke clean.
dyatlov_1959.slope.snowpit_done: The column broke clean, on the thin soft layer under the hard one: the wind-packed snow above slid off it like a lid. A [[slab]]. On this slope, below the cut, a small one would be enough to fall on a tent.
dyatlov_1959.cedar.tree: A great Siberian pine, the cedar of these forests, at the edge of the trees. Its lower branches are broken off up to five metres high, as if someone had climbed to look back up the slope, or for wood.
dyatlov_1959.cedar.fire: In the snow under the cedar, the black ring of a small fire of thin branches. It did not burn long.
dyatlov_1959.cedar.forest: Larch and spruce under snow, and a ravine beyond them where the snow lies four metres deep. The search will not reach its bottom until May.
dyatlov_1959.cedar.branch: A low branch of the cedar, broken.
dyatlov_1959.cedar.keeper_note: Tucked into the bark of the broken branch, a slip in the keeper's hand: "Nine people walked down a mountain in the dark, in a line, at a walking pace, and the world has been inventing monsters for them ever since. Write what the snow says, and leave the rest of the night to them."
dyatlov_1959.cedar.branch_done: The broken branch, where the keeper's slip was tucked.
dyatlov_1959.camp.casefile: The case file. Students and graduates of the Ural Polytechnic Institute, and their instructor: Igor Dyatlov, Yuri Doroshenko, Lyudmila Dubinina, Georgiy Krivonischenko, Alexander Kolevatov, Zinaida Kolmogorova, Rustem Slobodin, Nikolai Thibeaux-Brignolle, Semyon Zolotaryov. Yuri Yudin turned back, ill, on 28 January. They were on their way to [[otorten]]. Six died of the cold. Three of them, found in May in a ravine, had severe injuries to the chest and skull. The case is closed on "[[natural_force]]" that they could not overcome.
dyatlov_1959.camp.rumours: Notes of what is said in the camp and in the city. That [[mansi]] hunters attacked them; but there are no other tracks and no sign of a struggle, and the investigators set it aside. That orange spheres crossed the sky those weeks: [[aliens]], some will say. That [[weapons]] went wrong in the mountains.
dyatlov_1959.camp.cameras: Their cameras, taken from the tent, the films still in them. They go down to the investigators' darkroom in Ivdel.
dyatlov_1959.camp.cameras_done: The cameras, their films taken out to be developed.
dyatlov_1959.camp.radio: The search camp's radio, crackling: the base at Ivdel, the helicopter, the weather. February in the northern Urals: deep cold at night, and wind.
dyatlov_1959.camp.door_shut: The way down to Ivdel. Nothing to take there yet.
dyatlov_1959.camp.later: Papers that should not be here yet. Since 1959: [[radiation]] on some of their clothes, [[yeti]], weapons, spheres, infrasound; dozens of books. 2020: the prosecutor's office reopens the case and concludes that an avalanche most likely drove them from the tent. 2021: Johan Gaume and Alexander Puzrin show how a small slab could break on a slope under thirty degrees, hours after the cut was made for the tent, once the wind had piled snow above it, and how such a slab could injure people lying on a hard floor. Expeditions after them find the pass prone to avalanches. The authors add that no one really knows what happened that night.
dyatlov_1959.camp.routebook: The group's route book, stamped by the sports club at the start of the trip. The last pages are empty.
dyatlov_1959.camp.seal_needed: The route book's last page. Someone should write the last entry: what the snow says happened.
dyatlov_1959.darkroom.bench: The investigators' darkroom in Ivdel, under a red lamp: the films from their cameras, developed, and an enlarger to print them.
dyatlov_1959.darkroom.lamp: A red safelight. The paper does not see it.
dyatlov_1959.darkroom.prints: The prints, pinned up to dry: the river, the cache, the open slope, and the last one.
dyatlov_1959.darkroom.done: The last frame, printed right: before sunset on 1 February, figures with shovels digging into the slope below the shoulder to make a level place for the tent. [[cut]] in the snow.
dyatlov_1959.frame.1: Skis on the frozen river, January: the long way in, up the Auspiya.
dyatlov_1959.frame.2: The cache they built in the upper valley, food and spare gear left for the way back.
dyatlov_1959.frame.3: Climbing out of the trees onto the open slope, the afternoon of 1 February.
dyatlov_1959.frame.4: Before sunset: digging into the slope below the shoulder, to set the tent. The last frame on the roll.
dyatlov_1959.label.s1: A small {1} of snow broke above {2} made for the tent, and they walked down to {3}.
dyatlov_1959.label.done: The last entry is written in the route book, in the hand of someone who was not there.
dyatlov_1959.ending.pass: The pass where they died bears Igor Dyatlov's name.
dyatlov_1959.ending.record: In 2020 the case was closed again: an avalanche, most likely. What happened in the tent that night, no one saw.
hint.dyatlov_1959.start.1: Look at the tent, then at the tracks below it.
hint.dyatlov_1959.camp.1: The search camp is to the left of the slope.
hint.dyatlov_1959.camp.2: Read the case file, and take the cameras.
hint.dyatlov_1959.films.1: The films go to the darkroom, through the camp.
hint.dyatlov_1959.pit.1: A snow kit waits beside the tent.
hint.dyatlov_1959.pit.2: Dig the pit and test its layers.
hint.dyatlov_1959.later.1: New papers lie in the camp.
hint.dyatlov_1959.write_seal.1: The route book waits in the camp.
hint.dyatlov_1959.write_seal.2: Tap the route book on the table.
hint.dyatlov_1959.snowpit.1: Push in the largest thing first: if the fist goes in, the layer is fist-soft; if not, try four fingers, and so on.
hint.dyatlov_1959.snowpit.2: A weak layer is softer than the one above it. There are two such places; the column shows which one breaks.
hint.dyatlov_1959.snowpit.3: The thin soft layer under the wind slab, third from the top.
hint.dyatlov_1959.darkroom.1: On the test strip, choose the band where the snow is still white and the figures already dark.
hint.dyatlov_1959.darkroom.2: Too short and the print is grey and empty; too long and the snow goes grey. Each frame has its own band.
hint.dyatlov_1959.darkroom.3: Frames one and four at 8 seconds, frame two at 4, frame three at 16.
hint.dyatlov_1959.jar_label.1: What broke loose above the tent?
hint.dyatlov_1959.jar_label.2: Above what did it break, and where did they walk to?
episode.honnoji_1582.title: Honnō-ji, 1582
episode.honnoji_1582.teaser: A temple that burned with a ruler inside, a body never found, and a city that moved the temple and kept the legend.
honnoji_1582.dig.marker: A stone marker at the corner of the block: "Site of Honnō-ji". Behind it a school stood until 1992; now the block is being dug before something new is built. The chronicle's Shijō-bōmon is the street now called Takoyakushi.
honnoji_1582.dig.seal_needed: Below the temple's name the marker's face is still smooth, waiting for what is known.
honnoji_1582.dig.trench_wait: A deep trench under a tarp. The site office is still checking that it lies in the old temple's block.
honnoji_1582.dig.trench: The trench has found the moat. In its wall, the fill of four centuries, layer on layer, each with whatever was dropped into it.
honnoji_1582.dig.trench_done: The moat's section, every layer dated.
honnoji_1582.dig.sieves: Sieves on trestles, and buckets of grey sludge from the moat's bottom, washed through a spoonful at a time.
honnoji_1582.dig.strata_done: The black layer low in the moat, nothing in it later than the Ming: the fire of 1582. In its sludge, burnt roof tiles, their surfaces blistered: Honnō-ji, gone up in [[fire]]. Above it lies a later fire's ash, with coins of 1636 in it: Kyoto burned again, long after.
honnoji_1582.office.map_wait: A map of the city on the table, old street names and new. You need the two addresses first: the old temple's, and the new one's.
honnoji_1582.office.map: The map of central Kyoto, its streets named on a grid. Kyoto gives a place by a crossing and a direction: agaru, north; sagaru, south; higashi-iru, east; nishi-iru, west.
honnoji_1582.office.map_done: Two blocks marked on the map, a kilometre and a half apart.
honnoji_1582.office.streets_done: The temple of 1582 stood in the block between Rokkaku and Shijō-bōmon, Aburanokōji and Nishinotōin: the block being dug. The Honnō-ji visitors know stands far to the east, at Teramachi, where Hideyoshi moved it.
honnoji_1582.office.board: The permit board: an excavation at the site of the old Honnō-ji, 2007. Pinned below, a sketch of a fortified temple: a moat, a stone wall, a roofed mud wall. "Honnō-ji Castle", someone has written.
honnoji_1582.office.hats: Hard hats on pegs, mud on their brims.
honnoji_1582.finds.trays: Trays of finds, washed and bagged: sherds, coins, nails, and a great many broken roof tiles.
honnoji_1582.finds.chronicle: A paper that should not be here yet, from the past this time: the Shinchō Kōki of Ōta Gyūichi, who served Nobunaga. Before dawn on the 2nd day of the 6th month of 1582, [[akechi]] surrounded the temple with some thirteen thousand men. Nobunaga, with about seventy, shot with his bow until the strings broke, then fought with a spear, and was wounded. He withdrew inside as the temple burned, and took his own life.
honnoji_1582.finds.tile: A round eave tile, burnt, with the temple's name written in an older form of the character 能. Pulled from the moat's sludge.
honnoji_1582.finds.frois: A paper that should not be here yet: the Jesuit Luís Fróis, writing that year. Nobunaga had just washed his hands and face when an arrow struck him; he fought with a naginata, was hit in the arm, and shut himself in his chamber. What is known, Fróis wrote, is that of the man who made everyone tremble, not even a small hair remained that was not dust and ashes. Of his body, [[nothing]] was found.
honnoji_1582.finds.later: Papers that should not be here yet. Akechi held Kyoto for less than two weeks; Hideyoshi beat him at Yamazaki. That autumn Hideyoshi held Nobunaga's funeral at Daitoku-ji with no body: [[statue]] of fragrant wood was burned in its place. Yasuke, the African retainer who fought that day at Honnō-ji and at Nijō, was handed over by Akechi's men to the Jesuits. Why Akechi turned, more than fifty theories guess: [[hideyoshi]], [[ieyasu]], [[court]]. No record says.
honnoji_1582.teramachi.hall: The main hall of Honnō-ji at Teramachi, rebuilt here after the temple was moved. A bell sounds somewhere in the precinct.
honnoji_1582.teramachi.tower: A stone memorial to Nobunaga and those who died with him, offerings before it. A memorial, not a grave: there was nothing to bury.
honnoji_1582.teramachi.keeper_note: Behind the memorial, a slip in the keeper's hand: "They held a funeral and burned a statue in his place, and still people come here to look for him. Nothing was found, and nothing is what this jar must keep."
honnoji_1582.teramachi.tower_done: The memorial, where the keeper's slip lay.
honnoji_1582.teramachi.leaflet: A visitor's leaflet: "Honnō-ji, where Oda Nobunaga met his end". In small print: the temple was moved here, to [[teramachi]], in [[date_1591]], on Hideyoshi's order. Its address: Teramachi-Oike sagaru, on the east side.
honnoji_1582.teramachi.visitor: A guide's voice drifts across the court: since his body was never found, some say Nobunaga [[escaped]] the fire and lived out his days in secret.
honnoji_1582.find.yen: A ten-yen coin, first struck in 1951
honnoji_1582.find.sen: A Meiji one-sen coin, first struck in 1873
honnoji_1582.find.eiraku: An Eiraku Tsūhō, Ming cash, cast from 1408
honnoji_1582.find.kanei: A Kan'ei Tsūhō, the shogunate's coin, from 1636
honnoji_1582.find.imari: A sherd of Imari porcelain, made from the 1610s
honnoji_1582.find.ming: A sherd of Ming blue-and-white, from 1368
honnoji_1582.find.genpo: A Genpō Tsūhō, Song cash, cast from 1078
honnoji_1582.streets.old: The temple of 1582, from the chronicle and the site's marker: Rokkaku-Aburanokōji sagaru, higashi-iru, as far as Shijō-bōmon.
honnoji_1582.streets.new: Today's Honnō-ji, from the leaflet: Teramachi-Oike sagaru, on the east side.
honnoji_1582.label.s1: {1} turned on him, the temple went up in {2}, and of Nobunaga {3} was found.
honnoji_1582.label.done: The words are cut into the stone, below the temple's name.
honnoji_1582.ending.died: Oda Nobunaga died at Honnō-ji on the 2nd day of the 6th month of 1582, in the old temple between Rokkaku and Shijō-bōmon.
honnoji_1582.ending.why: Why Akechi Mitsuhide turned on him, no one knows.
hint.honnoji_1582.start.1: Read the marker at the corner of the dig.
hint.honnoji_1582.start.2: Then see the finds room, and today's Honnō-ji at Teramachi.
hint.honnoji_1582.office.1: The site office has the city map.
hint.honnoji_1582.office.2: Mark the two addresses: the old temple and the new.
hint.honnoji_1582.dig.1: The trench is in the right block: back to the dig.
hint.honnoji_1582.dig.2: Date the layers of the moat's section.
hint.honnoji_1582.frois.1: There is something new in the finds room.
hint.honnoji_1582.later.1: More papers are pinned up in the finds room.
hint.honnoji_1582.later.2: Read what came after the fire.
hint.honnoji_1582.write_seal.1: The marker waits at the corner of the dig.
hint.honnoji_1582.strata.1: Tap each find to read its earliest year. A layer is no older than its youngest find.
hint.honnoji_1582.strata.2: Nor is it older than the layer beneath it. Of the two black layers, only one can be from 1582.
hint.honnoji_1582.strata.3: From the top: 1951, 1636, 1636, 1610, 1408, 1078. The fire is the black layer with burnt tiles, fifth from the top.
hint.honnoji_1582.streets.1: Agaru is north, sagaru south, higashi-iru east and nishi-iru west of the crossing named.
hint.honnoji_1582.streets.2: Shijō-bōmon is the street now called Takoyakushi.
hint.honnoji_1582.streets.3: The old temple: east of Aburanokōji, between Rokkaku and Takoyakushi. The new: east of Teramachi, just south of Oike.
hint.honnoji_1582.jar_label.2: What took the temple, and what was found of Nobunaga?
episode.roanoke_1590.title: Roanoke, 1590
episode.roanoke_1590.teaser: A colony left on an island, a governor three years late, and one word cut into a post.
roanoke_1590.shore.grass: Grass and rotten trees still smoking along the shore. The fire the men saw through the woods last night burned here, and no one tended it.
roanoke_1590.shore.prints: Footprints in the sand, of two or three kinds, made in the night. Whoever walked here was gone before the boats came in.
roanoke_1590.shore.trumpet: A trumpet left on the boat's thwart. Last night the men sounded a call on it, then sang English tunes into the dark, one after another. Nothing answered.
roanoke_1590.shore.boat: The ship's boat, drawn up on the sand. Getting ashore cost seven men: a boat overset in the breakers at the inlet, and Captain Edward Spicer and six others drowned.
roanoke_1590.shore.keeper_note: Tucked in the trumpet's bell, a slip in the keeper's hand: "They sang all night to an empty island. Three years late is late, not lost: the word was left for him, and he could not follow it."
roanoke_1590.shore.trumpet_done: The trumpet, where the keeper's slip was.
roanoke_1590.hill.tree: On a tree at the brow of the hill, cut in fair Roman letters: CRO. Three letters, and no more. A word begun and left.
roanoke_1590.hill.view: From the hill the sound runs south between the banks and the main. Croatoan lies that way: Manteo's island, home of his people, who were friends to the English.
roanoke_1590.fort.palisade: Where the houses stood, only their places: the houses have been taken down, not burned. Round the site, a high palisade of great trees, with curtains and flankers, very like a fort. In the grass lie iron bars, two pigs of lead, four iron fowlers and shot for a saker, all overgrown with weeds.
roanoke_1590.fort.post: One of the chief posts at the right of the entrance has had its bark taken off, and five feet from the ground, in fair capital letters, is cut [[croatoan]]. Nothing is carved over it.
roanoke_1590.fort.seal_needed: Below the carved name the bare wood is still smooth: room for what is known.
roanoke_1590.chests.pit: At the end of an old trench, five chests that had been carefully hidden, dug up and broken open. Three are John White's own. His books are torn from their covers, the frames of his pictures and maps rotten with rain, his armour almost eaten through with rust.
roanoke_1590.chests.chart: Rolled in oiled cloth at the bottom of a chest, one chart has survived whole: White's own map of this coast, with its scale of miles and its compass rose. You take it to the ship.
roanoke_1590.chests.chart_done: The chests, emptied. The chart is on the cabin table now.
roanoke_1590.ship.journal: White's journal, open on the bunk: "At my coming away they were prepared to remove from Roanoke fifty miles into the main. We agreed that they should carve on the trees or posts the name of the place where they went; and if they went in distress, carve over it a [[cross]]." There is no cross on the post.
roanoke_1590.ship.table_wait: The cabin table, bare. White's own chart of the coast was in his chests ashore, if anything there survived.
roanoke_1590.ship.table_wait2: The chart is spread on the table. But what distances to measure? White's journal lies open on the bunk.
roanoke_1590.ship.table: White's chart, drawn as he drew it, with the west at the top. A pair of dividers lies on it.
roanoke_1590.ship.table_done: Two places pricked on the chart: Croatoan, and the meeting of the rivers inland.
roanoke_1590.dividers.croatoan: The token on the post: CROATOAN. Manteo's island lies some fifty miles south of Roanoke, down the banks. Mind the rose: on this chart, north is where it points.
roanoke_1590.dividers.main: "Fifty miles into the main": the plan they spoke of in 1587. The main lies west of Roanoke, across the sound.
roanoke_1590.ship.dividers_done: Croatoan, fifty miles south down the banks; and fifty miles into the main, where the rivers meet. On White's own map, now in London, a patch covers that very place.
roanoke_1590.ship.hatteras: Papers that should not be here yet. On Hatteras, once Croatoan, digs since 2009 have found a rapier's hilt, a slate with a letter scratched on it, English pottery among Croatoan things. Under the patch on White's map, light shows a fort drawn inland: [[site_x]], they call it. Both are argued over still.
roanoke_1590.ship.core: A paper from 1998, and with it a core drilled from an old bald cypress in the swamps near here. Its rings are wide in wet years and narrow in dry ones. A master chronology runs beside it, a ring for every year.
roanoke_1590.ship.rings_done: Dated. The three narrowest rings in a row: 1587, 1588, 1589. The worst [[drought]] in eight hundred years, in the very years the colony was left here. In a drought like that, corn fails, for the English and for those whose land this was.
roanoke_1590.ship.core_done: The core, its driest years marked: 1587 to 1589.
roanoke_1590.ship.core_wait: A roll of papers, tied. Measure the chart first; they will keep.
roanoke_1590.ship.later: Later papers. In 1937 a stone turned up by the Chowan River, carved as a message from Eleanor Dare; dozens more followed, [[dare_stones]], and in 1941 a magazine showed most were forged. A legend says Virginia Dare became [[white_doe]]. Some say the colony was wiped out by [[spanish]]; in 1612 William Strachey wrote of [[massacre]] by Powhatan's order, and no other record bears it out. And everywhere it is said the colony [[vanished]] without a trace.
roanoke_1590.label.s1: They carved {1} with no {2} of distress, in the worst {3} in eight hundred years.
roanoke_1590.label.done: The words are cut into the post, below the name.
roanoke_1590.ending.found: In August 1590 John White found CROATOAN cut into the fort's post, and no cross. Storm and a broken cable drove his ship away; he never reached Croatoan.
roanoke_1590.ending.after: Where the colonists went after that, the evidence is still argued over.
hint.roanoke_1590.start.1: Look round the shore, then climb the hill and go to the fort.
hint.roanoke_1590.start.2: Read the posts of the palisade.
hint.roanoke_1590.chests.1: By the fort, a pit by an old trench: White's chests.
hint.roanoke_1590.chests.2: Take what survived out to the ship.
hint.roanoke_1590.ship.1: In the cabin, read White's journal.
hint.roanoke_1590.ship.2: Then spread the chart on the table.
hint.roanoke_1590.dividers.1: Open the dividers to a span on the scale, pick a heading, then step.
hint.roanoke_1590.dividers.2: The rose shows north to the right: south is to the left, west is up.
hint.roanoke_1590.dividers.3: Croatoan: 10 miles, south, five steps. The main: 10 miles, west, five steps.
hint.roanoke_1590.core.1: A paper about a cypress core lies in the cabin now.
hint.roanoke_1590.core.2: Read it, and date the core.
hint.roanoke_1590.rings.1: Drag the core along the master; look for the same run of tall and short bars.
hint.roanoke_1590.rings.2: One short bar can match in two places; only the whole pattern fixes the core. Then bracket the three shortest in a row.
hint.roanoke_1590.rings.3: The core starts at 1579. The driest run: 1587 to 1589.
hint.roanoke_1590.later.1: More papers have come into the cabin.
hint.roanoke_1590.later.2: Read them; the legends are among them.
hint.roanoke_1590.write_seal.1: The post at the fort has room left on it.
hint.roanoke_1590.write_seal.2: What they carved, what they did not, and what they lived through.
hint.roanoke_1590.jar_label.1: The first word is the one on the post.
hint.roanoke_1590.jar_label.2: The second is what they would have carved over it in distress.
episode.franklin_1845.title: Franklin, 1845
episode.franklin_1845.teaser: Two ships that never came home, a note in a cairn, and a people who remembered where one went down.
franklin_1845.deck.ice_chart: Pinned by the bridge door, this year's ice chart. The northern search area, toward Victoria Strait, is shut by heavy ice; the team has moved south, to the waters off the Adelaide Peninsula.
franklin_1845.deck.shore: The low brown shore of the Adelaide Peninsula, September snow in its hollows. Somewhere off this coast, people here say, a ship went down long ago.
franklin_1845.hall.stories: The elders' recordings, kept in the hall. Off [[ugjulik]], the old accounts say, off the west shore of this peninsula, a ship was found afloat in the ice. Its men had left it. Hunters went aboard and took what they could use; inside lay a dead man. Later the ship sank. On the shore were the tracks of men walking south. In 1869 an Inuk, Inukpujijuk, marked the place on a visitor's chart.
franklin_1845.hall.map: A wall map of the land and the sea, with the Inuit names written on it and what they mean. Ugjulik: "there are bearded seals there", the sealing ground off the west shore of the Adelaide Peninsula, north and east of O'Reilly Island.
franklin_1845.hall.drum: A drum on the wall, its skin stretched on a wooden hoop.
franklin_1845.hall.keeper_note: Behind the drum, a slip in the keeper's hand: "For a hundred and sixty years the answer was told in this hall, in words that London would not hear. The ship lay where they said."
franklin_1845.hall.drum_done: The drum, where the keeper's slip was.
franklin_1845.survey.note: In a sleeve on the chart table, a paper from the past: the note left in a cairn at [[victory_point]] in 1848 and found in 1859, written all round its edges.
franklin_1845.note.print: Whoever finds this paper is requested to forward it to the Secretary of the Admiralty, London, with a note of the time and place at which it was found.
franklin_1845.note.body: 28 of May 1847. H.M. Ships Erebus and Terror wintered in the ice in Lat. 70°5' N, Long. 98°23' W. Having wintered in 1846–7 at Beechey Island, after having ascended Wellington Channel. Sir John Franklin commanding the expedition. All well.
franklin_1845.note.party: Party consisting of 2 officers and 6 men left the ships on Monday 24th May 1847. Gm. Gore, Lieut. Chas. F. Des Voeux, Mate.
franklin_1845.note.deserted: 25th April 1848. H.M. Ships Terror and Erebus were deserted on the 22nd April, 5 leagues NNW of this, having been beset since 12th Sept. 1846.
franklin_1845.note.franklin: Sir John Franklin died on the 11th June 1847, and the total loss by deaths in the expedition has been to this date 9 officers and 15 men.
franklin_1845.note.march: The officers and crews, consisting of 105 souls, under the command of Captain F. R. M. Crozier, landed here. F. R. M. Crozier, Captain. James Fitzjames, Captain. And start on tomorrow 26th for Back's Fish River.
franklin_1845.note.q_franklin: When did Sir John Franklin die?
franklin_1845.note.q_march: How many set out on foot, and for where?
franklin_1845.survey.margins_done: Read in the order it was written: "All well" in May 1847; Franklin dead that June, in [[date_1847]]; the ships deserted in April [[date_1848]], and 105 men setting out on foot. None reached the river.
franklin_1845.survey.note_done: The note in its sleeve, read all round.
franklin_1845.survey.hall_chart: A copy of Charles Francis Hall's chart, 1869. An Inuk named Inukpujijuk marked a ship on it in pencil: off the west shore of the Adelaide Peninsula, north and east of O'Reilly Island.
franklin_1845.survey.sonar_wait: The sonar screen, dark. Where to run the launch? First hear what the people of Gjoa Haven remember.
franklin_1845.survey.sonar_wait2: The accounts give the coast, but the search area is still wide and the hours are few. The helicopter crew is out on the islands; wait for word from them.
franklin_1845.survey.sonar: The survey grid off the peninsula, its lanes ruled east and west, north at the top. The hours of light are few this late in the season.
franklin_1845.survey.sonar_done: A long shape on the seabed, its shadow straight-edged: a ship. On 2 September 2014 the side-scan showed [[erebus]], about eleven metres down off the Adelaide Peninsula, where the Inuit had said a ship went down.
franklin_1845.survey.screen_done: The sonar screen, the wreck's echo held on it.
franklin_1845.survey.later: Later papers, and older ones. 1854: John Rae brings back Inuit accounts of the last men starving on their march, and relics bought from them; in London many refuse the Inuit word, Charles Dickens among them. 1984: the bodies at Beechey Island hold [[lead]], perhaps from the tins; later studies weigh it less. For long the ships are said to have been [[crushed]]. 2016: [[terror]] is found in Terror Bay, nearly whole, after a hunter from Gjoa Haven tells of timber seen through the ice.
franklin_1845.island.pintle: On the shore, by a large rock, an iron fitting: a pintle from a ship's davit, the small crane that held a boat. A little farther from the water, a wooden plug of the kind that stops a ship's hawse hole. Both of the Royal Navy's pattern, both from a ship that lay near.
franklin_1845.island.rocks: Lichen and purple saxifrage on grey rock. Ice grinds along the shore.
franklin_1845.island.helicopter: The ship's helicopter, its rotors still. The crew set down here on their way back from the camps ashore.
franklin_1845.label.s1: They left the ships in {1}; the Inuit said one went down off {2}, and {3} lay there.
franklin_1845.label.done: The words are written into the form's blanks.
franklin_1845.ending.found: In 2014 Erebus was found where the Inuit had said a ship went down; in 2016 Terror, where a hunter of Gjoa Haven had seen timber through the ice.
franklin_1845.ending.after: No one of the 129 came home.
hint.franklin_1845.start.1: Read the ice chart by the bridge door.
hint.franklin_1845.start.2: Then the note in the survey room.
hint.franklin_1845.hall.1: The launch runs to Gjoa Haven. Listen to the elders' recordings in the hall.
hint.franklin_1845.hall.2: Read the names on the wall map too.
hint.franklin_1845.island.1: The helicopter crew set down on a small island.
hint.franklin_1845.survey.1: Now run the sonar in the survey room.
hint.franklin_1845.survey.2: The accounts, the place names and the island all point one way.
hint.franklin_1845.margins.1: Turn the sheet: each passage can be read only when it stands upright.
hint.franklin_1845.margins.2: The 1847 note in the middle says "All well". The answers are in the 1848 hand round the edges.
hint.franklin_1845.margins.3: Deserted: up the right side. Franklin: upside down along the top. The march: down the left side.
hint.franklin_1845.sonar.1: The accounts: off the west shore of the Adelaide Peninsula, north and east of O'Reilly Island, south of Grant Point.
hint.franklin_1845.sonar.2: Do not spend the hours far north toward Victory Point. The pintle washed up on an island close to her.
hint.franklin_1845.sonar.3: Run the sixth lane from the top and mark the long echo with the straight shadow.
hint.franklin_1845.later.1: Papers have come into the survey room.
hint.franklin_1845.later.2: Read them; the old dismissals are among them.
hint.franklin_1845.write_seal.1: A fresh Admiralty form waits in the survey room.
hint.franklin_1845.write_seal.2: When they left the ships, where the Inuit said one sank, and which ship lay there.
hint.franklin_1845.jar_label.1: The year is in the 1848 hand on the note.
hint.franklin_1845.jar_label.2: The place is the Inuit name: the bearded seals.
